title: Hubble Spies a Glittering Gathering of Stars
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6558, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Stars in a rich variety of hues throng this Hubble image of NGC 6558, a globular cluster. Some of the brightest carry prominent diffraction spikes, imaging artefacts made when starlight interacts with the structure inside the telescope.

NGC 6558 lies about 23 000 light years away in Sagittarius, nearer our galaxy's centre than we are. Globular clusters are tightly bound collections of anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars, found in many kinds of galaxies, and as NGC 6558 shows, their stars can be packed very densely.

They are also natural laboratories. A globular cluster's stars were born at roughly one time with a similar starting composition, so astronomers can compare how various stars develop when starting conditions match. The picture belongs to a set of observations of globular clusters in the inner Milky Way, aimed at understanding how those clusters form and change.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the cluster through visible (F606W) and near-infrared (F814W) filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the spikes around bright stars are an artefact of the telescope, not something in the sky.
